```{r}
#| label: options
#| include: false
options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
```

Contact risks model transmission between groups of individuals within a household.
Unlike group risks, contact risks are pairwise: they scale the person-to-person rate from one member to another.
By default, risks are absolute, each pair introducing its own parameter.
If a reference pair is introduced (constant 1), all other contact pairs become relative to it.
We illustrate the API on the influenza survey in Matsumoto, which reports final sizes together with the family role of each member.
To simplify this walkthrough, we regroup members as follows:

```{r}
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme()
set_housepi_summary(cri_level = 0.95)
set.seed(42)

#| label: recall-original-data
hh_model <- new_housepi_model(model = "final-size")

# group together children and parents
dataset <- flu_2014_matsumoto |>
  dplyr::mutate(member = dplyr::case_when(
    member %in% c("student", "sibling") ~ "child",
    member %in% c("father", "mother") ~ "parent",
    .default = member
  )) |>
  dplyr::filter(hh_id %in% sample(unique(hh_id), 500L))

# associate the data
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  add_data_wide(dataset)

table(dataset$member)
```

# Define absolute contact risks

To associate contact risks to models that encode them, we call `add_contact_risk()`.
This reads one or more covariate columns and introduces a parameter per pair.

```{r}
#| label: load-model-data
hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk("member") |>
  get_contact_risks()
```

Contact risks are paired, `from_member` (the infector), `to_member` (the infectee).
Here `n` counts the ordered pairs observed in the data, and `param_name` names the associated parameter.
Pairs that never occur are dropped.
The `rule_group` column matters once rules overlap (see [strata tables](#strata-tables-and-specificity-rules)).

By default, a pair and its reverse share one parameter, so `parent` infecting `child` and viceversa will be equal.
Set `symmetric = FALSE` to let them differ.

```{r}
#| label: symmetry-count
# disable symmetric risks
hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk("member", symmetric = FALSE) |>
  get_contact_risks()
```

```{r}
#| label: count-new-params
#| include: false
# count the number of parameters associated to contact risks
count_ctr <- function(x) length(unique(get_contact_risks(x)$param_name))
c_diff <- count_ctr(add_contact_risk(hh_model, "member", symmetric = FALSE)) -
  count_ctr(add_contact_risk(hh_model, "member"))
```

Dropping symmetry splits every mixed pair in two, leaving the homologous pairs alone, and costing `r c_diff` new parameters to infer.

# A reference pair makes the risks relative

Parameters associated to risks are collected alongside other declarations.
```{r}
#| label: parameters-default
hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk("member") |>
  get_parameters()
```

Parameters inherit shared MCMC default configurations as in group risks (see [Group risks](group_risks.html)).
By default, all contact risks are absolute and the baseline transmission `beta` non identifiable, so the model fixes it at 1.
Instead, naming a `reference` pair makes it the unit, `beta` is freed, and every other parameter reads as a relative risk to the reference.

```{r}
#| label: custom-reference
hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk(
    "member",
    reference = c(from_member = "child", to_member = "other")
  ) |>
  get_contact_risks()
```

Passing an un-prefixed name applies the same value to both sides.

```{r}
#| label: reference-shorthand
dataset |>
  new_housepi_model("final-size") |>
  add_contact_risk("member", reference = "parent") |>
  get_contact_risks()
```

Ask for `".auto"` to take the pair with the largest sample size, which here is parent to child:

```{r}
#| label: auto-reference
hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk("member", reference = ".auto") |>
  get_contact_risks()
```

# Strata tables and specificity rules

While `by` associates parameters automatically to all covariates, a fine grained stratification can be provided with a `strata` table.
In `strata`, covariate columns say which pairs each row matches, and `param_name` says which parameter they get.
An `NA` cell is a catch-all that matches any value, unless a more specific rule exists.
A row with all covariate cells set to `NA` is the least specific rule possible, so it is beaten by every other rule and covers whatever remains.

```{r}
#| label: strata-table
strata <- tibble::tribble(
  ~from_member, ~to_member, ~param_name,       ~value,
  "child",      "parent",   "child_to_parent", 2.5,
  NA,           NA,         ".reference",      NA
)
model_strata <- hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk(strata = strata)

# show contact risk definitions
model_strata |>
  get_contact_risks()

# extract the first household with all classes
hh_id <- model_strata$data_wide |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::n_distinct(member) > 2, .by = hh_id) |>
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 1) |>
  dplyr::pull(hh_id)

# inspect how the definitions reach the given household
state <- model_strata |>
  inspect_house_state(hh_id)
# recall the data associated to household '1133'
state$data_wide
# export loaded contact risks
state$contact_risks
```

Contacts between a child and a parent got a parameter `child_to_parent`.
By default, the table gets symmetrized, so the opposite direction is matched by the same rule.
Everything else fell on the reference.
Here we used `tibble::tribble` for cleanness, but any object ultimately a `data.frame` will do.


The `params` argument gives one MCMC setup per parameter; a bare number pins it, which is what we use here to read the rates off a household.
`inspect_house_state()` returns everything the engine holds for one household, including the matrix of pairwise rates it multiplies `beta` by.

## Ambiguous rules are rejected

Rules that key on different columns cannot be ranked against each other.
The `rule_group` column of `get_contact_risks()` reports which rules were compared together, and a catch-all rule that straddles two groups raises an error instead of picking a winner:

```{r}
#| label: strata-ambiguous
#| error: true
half_keyed <- tibble::tribble(
  ~from_member, ~to_member, ~param_name,
  "child",      NA,         "ctr_child",
  NA,           NA,         ".reference"
)

# not ambiguos definiton for symmetric risks
hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk(strata = half_keyed, symmetric = FALSE) |>
  get_contact_risks()

# ambiguos definiton for symmetric risks
hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk(strata = half_keyed, symmetric = TRUE) |>
  get_contact_risks()
```

Keying the first rule on both columns, as in the tables above, removes the choice and the definition goes through.

# Inference

No reference was given, so the three rates are absolute and `beta` is held at `1`.
The relative parametrization estimates `beta` alongside the rates, and on this survey the chains mix slowly along the direction that trades one against the other, so the absolute one is the cheaper read.
`run_simulation()` holds `beta` at the same `1`, so a survey generated from these draws comes from the model that was fitted.

```{r}
#| label: inference-contact-risks
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Five trace plots of the MCMC draws: the community risk alpha, the
#|  household-size exponent gamma, and the three pairwise transmission rates
#|  between children and parents. Four chains are overlaid across iterations.
hh_model <- hh_model |>
  add_contact_risk("member") |>
  add_parameter(import = "template")

results <- hh_model |>
  run_inference(progress = 4)
results |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace()
```

The from/to table returned by `get_contact_risks()` joins the draws back onto the pair they belong to, which lays the estimates out as a contact matrix:

```{r}
#| label: contact-matrix-plot
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: >
#|  A three by three matrix of posterior transmission rates, infector on the
#|  horizontal axis and infectee on the vertical one. Each cell carries its
#|  median rate and credible interval.
library(ggplot2)

hh_model |>
  get_contact_risks() |>
  dplyr::rename(variable = param_name) |>
  dplyr::left_join(summarise_draws(results), by = "variable") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = from_member, y = to_member, fill = median)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = format_credible_interval(median, q2.5, q97.5, "%s\n[%s, %s]")),
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(x = "infector", y = "infectee")
```

We obtain that transmission between members of the same class is much larger than across classes.
